item.research_question: How can a single-phase high-entropy intermetallic alloy be designed to overcome the inherent brittleness of traditional intermetallics and achieve both high strength and extensive plasticity at room temperature and high homologous temperatures?
item.processing_route: Arc-melting high-purity raw materials (>99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, remelted at least five times, drop-cast into a copper mold, homogenized at 1000 °C for 24 h, and water quenched
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial compression from room temperature to ~0.9Tm (1582 K) at 1 × 10−3 s−1; microcompression on 1 μm diameter pillars at RT, 573 K, and 673 K; in situ STEM at RT and 573 K
key_findings: Yield strength of ~1.5 GPa with plastic strain of ~8% at room temperature, which is about eight times that of conventional B2 alloys like NiAl and CoTi.
The alloy exhibits no precipitous thermal softening between homologous temperatures of 0.5 and 0.7, maintaining strength and strain hardening up to ~0.7Tm.
Micropillars with [100], [110], and [111] orientations show similar yield strength and elastic stiffness, indicating isotropic-like mechanical behavior.
Two slip systems, {110}<111> and {010}<100>, were identified with critical resolved shear stresses of 1235 ± 39 MPa and 1176 ± 245 MPa, respectively, differing by only 5%.
At room temperature, deformation induces local amorphization within slip bands, whereas at temperatures above 573 K, deformation results in dense dislocation forests without amorphization.
The velocity ratio of screw-to-edge dislocations was calculated to be ~0.6 at 300 K, significantly higher than the ~0.2 ratio in brittle BCC metals like tungsten.
item.mechanism: Severe lattice distortion caused by atomic size and electronic property misfit mitigates atomic bonding differences along various crystal orientations, enabling dislocation multiplicity and isotropic behavior. Dislocation gliding disturbs the local chemical order, causing structural instability that leads to amorphization at low temperatures and the formation of local crystal-like order (dynamic hardening) at high temperatures, which impedes subsequent dislocation gliding and stabilizes plastic flow.
item.limitations: The text notes that fracture at low temperatures may occur within amorphized regions and that the plastic strain at room temperature can vary (up to 27%) depending on machine stiffness, though this variability disappears at higher temperatures.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that manipulating the lattice distortion by adjusting the ratio of Co to Ni is a topic that warrants further research but is out of the scope of the current work.
quotes: Unlike conventional intermetallics, this high-entropy alloy features a highly distorted crystalline lattice with complex chemical order, leading to multiple slip systems and high flow stress.
Our HEIA does not experience precipitous thermal softening at homologous temperatures between 0.5 and 0.7.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity triggers local structural transition in the wake of passing dislocations, leading to amorphization at low temperatures and dynamic hardening at high temperatures.

Question: How can a single-phase high-entropy intermetallic alloy be designed to overcome the inherent brittleness of traditional intermetallics and achieve both high strength and extensive plasticity at room temperature and high homologous temperatures?. System: (CoNi)50(TiZrHf)50 (at. %) single-phase B2 high-entropy intermetallic alloy. Processing: Arc-melting high-purity raw materials (>99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, remelted at least five times, drop-cast into a copper mold, homogenized at 1000 °C for 24 h, and water quenched. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression from room temperature to ~0.9Tm (1582 K) at 1 × 10−3 s−1; microcompression on 1 μm diameter pillars at RT, 573 K, and 673 K; in situ STEM at RT and 573 K. Findings: Yield strength of ~1.5 GPa with plastic strain of ~8% at room temperature, which is about eight times that of conventional B2 alloys like NiAl and CoTi.; The alloy exhibits no precipitous thermal softening between homologous temperatures of 0.5 and 0.7, maintaining strength and strain hardening up to ~0.7Tm.; Micropillars with [100], [110], and [111] orientations show similar yield strength and elastic stiffness, indicating isotropic-like mechanical behavior.; Two slip systems, {110}<111> and {010}<100>, were identified with critical resolved shear stresses of 1235 ± 39 MPa and 1176 ± 245 MPa, respectively, differing by only 5%.; At room temperature, deformation induces local amorphization within slip bands, whereas at temperatures above 573 K, deformation results in dense dislocation forests without amorphization.; The velocity ratio of screw-to-edge dislocations was calculated to be ~0.6 at 300 K, significantly higher than the ~0.2 ratio in brittle BCC metals like tungsten.. Mechanism: Severe lattice distortion caused by atomic size and electronic property misfit mitigates atomic bonding differences along various crystal orientations, enabling dislocation multiplicity and isotropic behavior. Dislocation gliding disturbs the local chemical order, causing structural instability that leads to amorphization at low temperatures and the formation of local crystal-like order (dynamic hardening) at high temperatures, which impedes subsequent dislocation gliding and stabilizes plastic flow.. Limitations: The text notes that fracture at low temperatures may occur within amorphized regions and that the plastic strain at room temperature can vary (up to 27%) depending on machine stiffness, though this variability disappears at higher temperatures.. Future work: The authors suggest that manipulating the lattice distortion by adjusting the ratio of Co to Ni is a topic that warrants further research but is out of the scope of the current work.. Quote: "Unlike conventional intermetallics, this high-entropy alloy features a highly distorted crystalline lattice with complex chemical order, leading to multiple slip systems and high flow stress."
